example.answer: The investment grows to $16,470.09, earning $6,470.09 in interest.
example.problem: You invest $10,000 at 5% annual interest, compounded monthly, and leave it for 10 years. What is it worth?
example.title: Ten years of monthly compounding

faqs.a: Divide the annual rate by the number of compounding periods per year, then raise to the power of total periods: A = P(1 + r/n)^(n×t). This calculator does every step for you.
faqs.q: What is the formula for compound interest?

faqs.a: More frequent compounding earns slightly more because interest starts earning interest sooner. On $10,000 at 5% for 10 years, yearly compounding gives $16,288.95 while monthly gives $16,470.09, a difference of $181.14.
faqs.q: Does compounding monthly really beat compounding yearly?

faqs.a: The effective annual rate (EAR) is the rate that yearly compounding would need to match your result: (1 + r/n)^n − 1. At 5% compounded monthly, the EAR is about 5.12%. It is the fairest way to compare accounts with different compounding frequencies.
faqs.q: What is the effective annual rate?

faqs.a: Yes, if your balance stays the same. Real investments gain and lose value, and inflation eats purchasing power, so treat the result as a projection, not a promise.
faqs.q: Can I use this to project stock market growth?

formula.label: Compound interest
formula.note: P = principal, r = annual rate as a decimal, n = compounds per year, t = years

formula.label: Interest earned
formula.note: The final amount minus what you started with

howItWorks: Simple interest only ever pays you on your original deposit, but compound interest pays you on your deposit plus all the interest already earned. Each compounding period, the balance grows by the period rate, and the next period's interest is calculated on that bigger balance. That is why the growth curves upward instead of in a straight line.

The calculator applies the standard formula A = P(1 + r/n)^(n×t): your principal times one plus the per-period rate, raised to the total number of periods. It also shows the effective annual rate so you can compare accounts honestly. These are mathematical projections, not financial advice: real investments carry risk, fees, and taxes that this calculator does not include.
intro: See how savings or investments grow when interest earns interest. Enter a starting amount, an annual rate, and how many years, then choose how often the interest compounds.

mistakes.text: The formula needs the rate as a decimal. Entering 5 as the rate means 500%. Always divide the percent by 100 first: 5% → 0.05.
mistakes.title: Using 5 instead of 0.05 for the rate

mistakes.text: With yearly compounding n = 1, so the per-period rate is the full annual rate. Only divide by 12 or 4 when the interest actually compounds monthly or quarterly.
mistakes.title: Dividing the rate when compounding is yearly

mistakes.text: On $10,000 at 5% for 10 years, simple interest earns $5,000 but monthly compounding earns $6,470.09. Confusing the two understates long-term growth by a wide margin.
mistakes.title: Mixing up simple and compound interest

mistakes.text: 5% compounded monthly is not quite 5% per year of growth: the effective annual rate is about 5.12%. Use the EAR, not the headline rate, when comparing two accounts.
mistakes.title: Ignoring the effective annual rate
